description: Database-backed worker backend for Django's Tasks framework (django.tasks), on Django 5.2 LTS and later. Background tasks run on the database you already have. No broker to provision or back up.
rules: Requires Python 3.12+ and Django 5.2+. Install with pip install django-ox; on Django 5.2 LTS use django-ox[backport] for the django-tasks backport. Django 6.0+ ships the Tasks framework in core.
Add django_ox to INSTALLED_APPS; set TASKS = {"default": {"BACKEND": "django_ox.backend.OxBackend"}}. Run python manage.py migrate django_ox before starting workers, never from a worker.
Import task from django.tasks on Django 6.0+, or django_tasks on 5.2. Use @task and .enqueue(...). Task modules must be importable in workers running the producer's code. async def tasks work.

OxBackend accepts provisional max_attempts, backoff and timeout kwargs on Django 6.1 or Django 5.2 with django-tasks 0.12+. Django 6.0 rejects these kwargs at import; bare @task works. Task.using() cannot set policy fields.

Run python manage.py ox_worker separately from the web server; tasks need a running worker. --queues a,b restricts its queues. The worker polls; --interval defaults to 1.0 seconds. There is no LISTEN/NOTIFY.

enqueue() is one INSERT on the OxTask write alias. For a joint commit, open transaction.atomic() there and write the caller's rows there too; bare atomic() uses default. Do not wrap enqueue in transaction.on_commit().

Execution is at-least-once: write idempotent tasks using database state, not memory flags. Task functions run outside a transaction; open transaction.atomic() inside a task for atomic writes or select_for_update().

django_ox.bulk.enqueue_many(task, [(args, kwargs), ...]) returns results in input order: one INSERT per 1,000 rows, one transaction. Set queue, priority and run_after once with task.using(...), not per call.
QUEUES sits beside OPTIONS in TASKS, not inside OPTIONS. It defaults to ["default"]; [] permits any queue name. Inside OPTIONS it is silently ignored. Schedule settings also live under OPTIONS.

OPTIONS defaults: MAX_ATTEMPTS=3, LOCK_TIMEOUT=300, BACKOFF_INITIAL=5, BACKOFF_MAX=600, TASK_TIMEOUT=None, TASK_TIMEOUTS={}, TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE=30, SCHEDULES={}. Durations are seconds. Use a non-bool integer 1..32767 for MAX_ATTEMPTS.
PostgreSQL claims use one UPDATE with a SKIP LOCKED subquery and RETURNING; MySQL 8+ uses SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. SQLite and databases without SKIP LOCKED use an atomic compare-and-set UPDATE.

An attempt is consumed at claim, including when a worker dies. max_attempts is stored at enqueue; later declarations do not alter that budget. Backoff and timeout use the worker's live task declaration on each attempt.

Default retry delay after attempt n is min(BACKOFF_INITIAL * 2 ** (n - 1), BACKOFF_MAX), without jitter. A callback may return an uncapped delay or None to stop. Invalid results or callback errors use the default formula.

LOCK_TIMEOUT limits missed lease renewal, not task runtime. Renewal is scheduled every LOCK_TIMEOUT / 3 seconds and needs database access. A live worker can lose its lease if renewal cannot reach the database in time.

Timeout precedence: task timeout, TASK_TIMEOUTS[queue], TASK_TIMEOUT. A task timeout applies even on a queue exempted with None; a task cannot disable an inherited limit. Each attempt gets a fresh timeout.

At the deadline, sync tasks receive django_ox.exceptions.TaskTimeout, subject to tracing exceptions; async tasks are cancelled. django_ox.deadline() and django_ox.remaining() expose the attempt deadline inside a task.

A thread still running TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE seconds after its deadline is recorded as failed; the worker exits 75 for supervisor restart. This stuck-thread path uses worker backoff without calling user callbacks.

With sys.settrace or active sys.monitoring, timeouts_backstop_only logs: no sync exception is injected. A sync return within grace keeps its outcome; otherwise the task fails and worker recycles. Async cancellation still occurs at deadline.

Use django_ox.testing.ImmediateBackend or DummyBackend for policy-bearing tasks; stock test backends can reject or ignore policy. Both validate but enforce no retries, backoff or timeouts. Test enforcement with a real worker.

ox_worker --concurrency N runs a thread pool in one process; --processes N runs N workers under one supervisor. Each process has its own database connections. Use --processes N --concurrency 1 for CPU-bound work.

A dead worker process restarts after one second, doubling to 30 seconds. More than five deaths of one slot within a minute stops the supervisor with exit 1. Allow for replacement backoff in heartbeat probes.

PostgreSQL pool: at least concurrency + 1 pooled connections per worker; add a spare for fallback under full load. Budget up to max_size + 2 server connections per process/alias normally, or max_size + 3 during stop-time recovery.
When upgrading to 1.8.0 with Django's PostgreSQL pool, use psycopg_pool 3.3.0+ for the pool-drain fix; 3.3.3 is recommended. Review WARNING connection_pool_cannot_drain.

OPTIONS["SCHEDULES"] uses cron or every, never both. every is seconds or timedelta with optional phase and fixed-instant ticks. Every worker dispatches; a unique constraint deduplicates tick enqueue. No scheduler process is needed.

After an outage, enqueue only the most recent missed tick, skipping older ones. New schedules never fire before creation. Retiming stored schedules starts from the change; re-enabling does not replay missed ticks. Tick execution remains at-least-once.

For admin-editable schedules, set OPTIONS["SCHEDULE_SOURCE"] to "django_ox.stored.DatabaseScheduleSource". Rows name keys exposed by @schedulable or OPTIONS["SCHEDULABLE_TASKS"], never arbitrary import paths.

@schedulable requires its module to be imported; installed apps' tasks modules are imported. Write with django_ox.stored.create_schedule, create_schedules or update_schedule; objects.create() skips validation and leaves activation stale.

django_ox.stored.create_schedules(rows, *, user=None) is public and stable in 1.8.0. It creates many stored schedules all-or-nothing, returning a list of OxSchedule objects or [] for empty input. Names must be unique within the input.
create_schedules: one ValidationError lists validation failures by row index, name, field and message. A non-mapping row or unsupported key raises TypeError immediately.

create_schedules: PermissionDenied separately names denied rows. Database refusals at check or write raise for one row; a concurrent name conflict raises IntegrityError and rolls back the entire call.
ox_import_beat_schedules reads django-celery-beat's database scheduler tables: PeriodicTask, CrontabSchedule and IntervalSchedule.

The importer first shipped in 1.2.0 and was rebuilt in 1.8.0. It prints one all-or-nothing create_schedules call for review and application, reads Celery crontab grammar and lists untranslatable rows with named reasons.

For ox_import_beat_schedules, --database selects the django-celery-beat source alias, defaulting to the OxSchedule read alias. --beat-timezone ZONE supplies beat's timezone. Review output and named reasons before applying it.

1.8.0 needs no new migration. If you applied importer output from 1.2.0-1.7.0, re-check crontabs restricting both day fields or using zones other than Django's TIME_ZONE. See https://oxpull.com/django-ox/changelog/.
Upgrade 1.2.0-1.7.0 for medium advisory GHSA-gq8r-4ccg-vxcr, fixed in 1.8.0. Invalid stored schedule rows are skipped and logged; other schedules and queued tasks continue.

1.8.0 fixes a 1.7.0 MySQL lease-renewal defect for a shared Worker when one caller runs run_once() inside its own atomic block. Other tasks could lose leases and run twice. PostgreSQL and separate Workers were unaffected.

path("ox/", include("django_ox.urls")) exposes GET /ox/metrics without authentication; protect it or restrict network access. django_ox.metrics.collector() registers the same gauges with a prometheus_client registry.

The /ox/metrics gauges are django_ox_tasks{queue,status}, django_ox_ready_tasks, django_ox_oldest_ready_age_seconds, django_ox_last_claim_age_seconds, django_ox_throughput_per_minute and django_ox_failure_rate.

Use ox_health database and queue thresholds for dependency checks and fleet alerts, not per-container liveness. --worker-timeout measures recent claims across workers; an idle queue can fail and another worker can make it pass.

For local liveness, pair ox_worker --heartbeat-file PATH with ox_health --heartbeat-file PATH and matching --processes N. Use a private absolute path per container. A pass proves loop advancement, not task progress or renewal.

Size heartbeat freshness for startup, poll interval, reap/dispatch, one claim and margin; include pool timeout (default 30 s). There is no overall poll-pass deadline. A database hang can trigger fleet-wide liveness restart storms.
ox_prune --older-than 7d deletes old SUCCESSFUL and DISCARDED rows. FAILED and LOST stay unless --include-failed. READY, RUNNING and WAITING are never deleted.

django_ox.actions.retry(result_id) requeues FAILED or LOST for one more attempt. discard(result_id) closes READY, WAITING, FAILED or LOST without running it. Both return bool; neither touches RUNNING tasks.

OxTask.Status.WAITING is never written by django-ox itself. Workers do not claim it, ox_prune does not delete it and retry skips it. It reads as READY through django.tasks. Oxpull Pro workflows write and release it.

ox_worker, ox_prune and database-mode ox_health take --database, defaulting to the OxTask write alias; overrides are not checked against routing. Keep all django-ox tables together. ox_health --heartbeat-file refuses --database.

Batches, unique tasks, rate limiting and workflows belong to Oxpull Pro, a paid Django 6.0+ add-on at https://oxpull.com/. Free create_schedules creates stored schedules. stats and ox_health are free.
Stored schedule start_time is its activation boundary. starting_deadline_seconds drops overly late ticks and logs schedule_tick_dropped with lateness; the default is no deadline.

Alert on schedule_dispatch_error and schedule_dispatch_failed; inspect failures and suppressed, not just log counts. manage.py check cannot establish database acceptance. ox_worker --batch exit 0 does not prove every schedule enqueued.

SIGTERM/SIGINT request drain then exit 0; a second signal forces exit 130. A main loop hung in a database call cannot begin draining until it returns. If the process cannot act on signals, SIGKILL is needed.

For queued tests, keep OxBackend and use provisional django_ox.testing.run_tasks(). It runs due attempts with retries/backoff, not automatic timeouts, renewal, schedules or reconcilers. Use TransactionTestCase for worker autocommit behaviour.
